items.point: Memory note summarising the day's KeyLab work

evidence.front: Prior art near the KeyLab vision: steal the best idea from each product, and find what is genuinely new. The vision is a liberated KeyLab 88 mk3 with live chord recognition on its pads and screen, beat-synced lights from any audio, VST hosting with FL Studio preset round-trip, and web pages (piano visualizer, VFX bench) that drive the keyboard.
evidence.summary: Each piece of this vision already exists somewhere, done well. What no one ships is all of it together on one keyboard. Scale and chord lighting is common: NI Light Guide, Push, Maschine, Launchkey Chord Map, and the KeyLab's own Chord and Scale modes. Instrument metadata driving the controller is NKS. Hosting is Carla, Pedalboard and DawDreamer. Audio-reactive light is LedFx, WLED and Hue. Chord timelines are Chordify and Hooktheory. Pad light shows are Launchpad and Apollo Studio. Every vendor controller only names chords from its own chord-generator modes. Showing the name of a freely played chord on a controller screen exists only as a third-party Max for Live hack for Push. I found no product that drives controller pads from arbitrary system audio, lets a visual web app write live content to a keyboard's screen and lights, or round-trips FL .fst presets through a standalone host. Those three gaps plus one shared harmonic colour language are the real novelty. The biggest practical finding is that the KeyLab mk3 protocol is no longer ours alone. Bitwig's own KeyLab mk3 extension is MIT-licensed, open, and was updated 2026-10-21. An MIT reverse-engineering repo (saxofonbrian/keylab-mk3-sysex, created 2026-09-07) documents the screen widgets and a hard rule: two back-to-back screen packets race and one is dropped, so space them about 60 ms apart. Bitwig's source also uses a different first LED byte (0x04, where our FL-derived code uses 0x02). It also defines blink and pulse states that, if the firmware honours them, would let the device animate beat lights itself. Three design constraints follow. First, the KeyLab LCD is a templated widget screen (text lines, lists, popups, icons), not a framebuffer like Push 2's 960x160, so rich timelines belong on the web page. Second, Windows MIDI Services multi-client is running on this machine (MidiSrv was Running when checked 2026-10-22), and Chrome now puts all Web MIDI behind a permission prompt. Pages, FL and a Python daemon writing the screen together would therefore collide silently, so use NI's pattern: one local agent owns the hardware and pages send it intents. Third, Pedalboard, PyFLP, LedFx and Carla are GPL, and beatsync.py already imports the GPLv3+ aubio-ledfx package inside the Apache-2.0 repo.

items.point: Already in the repo (the baseline the survey is measured against)
items.detail: chordview shows the chord name on the LCD and lights the pads, coloured by interval role and chord quality (ROLE_COLORS and QUALITY_COLORS). beatsync detects the beat from WASAPI loopback audio with aubio and reads the title from Windows SMTC; Spotify's beat API returns 403 for new apps. ledframe is a diffing pad renderer under a measured 12-packet burst ceiling. The piano page already has a 3D virtual twin of the KeyLab whose pads and screen react. A grep of arsenal/ found no VST hosting and no .fst preset handling; the .fst files in arsenal/fl/vfx are FL VFX Script tutorials, not presets. The harmony and practice side of Scaler, Captain, Hooktheory, Chordify and Synthesia is already surveyed in research/in-flight/ultimate-practice-tool-2026-09-14/products.md sections 2.1, 2.3 and 2.6, so this pass covers only their hardware and lighting angle.

items.point: NI Kontrol S MK3, Light Guide and NKS. Steal: the instrument declares and the hardware draws. Key zones, key switches and named parameter pages come from per-plugin metadata, and one background agent owns the screens and lights for every host.
items.detail: What NI does: the Light Guide shows split zones and colour-coded key switches from NKS instruments. In Scale mode the root is bright and other scale notes dimmed; Chord mode works through the Harmonizer. The Performance view puts the key parameters on a few pages; the Edit view exposes every parameter. An .nksf preset is a RIFF file with four chunks: NISI (summary), NICA (controller pages), PLID (plugin ID) and PCHK (the plugin state). All but PCHK are MessagePack. So NICA is a ready-made, readable map of encoder pages for any plugin that has NKS presets, and Arturia lists the KeyLab mk3 as NKS-compatible. NIHostIntegrationAgent is the one daemon that writes text and images to the screens and coordinates the Light Guide. What it does NOT do: name a freely played chord on the screen, react lights to outside audio, or light third-party NKS plugins without the Komplete Kontrol software. NKS2 on non-NI hardware is closer to NKS1.

items.point: Maschine MK3. Steal: colour belongs to the sound. A sound's colour is set once and carries through to pads, screen and software. In note modes the root and its octaves are fully lit, other pads dim, and chord tones white.
items.detail: For us: a hosted instrument or preset would carry one identity colour, used as the pad base, the LCD accent and the theme colour on the web page. What it does NOT do: recognise chords you play freely, react to outside audio, or host anything outside NI's software.

items.point: Ableton Push 2/3. Steal two things: a published, exact display and LED spec, and its pad-colour grammar. In key, the root takes the track colour, scale notes are white and notes outside the scale are off. Pads can also run their own clock-synced animation.
items.detail: Push 2 display: 960x160 pixels in RGB565, 60 fps, double-buffered, and it goes black if no frame arrives for 2 s (a built-in dead-man switch worth copying for our LCD and pads). LEDs: a 128-entry palette with white balance; MIDI channel 0 sets a static colour and channels 1-15 give one-shot, pulse or blink transitions synced to MIDI clock. The 'root takes the track colour' rule is the adaptive-colour idea: the KeyLab's root pad would take the colour of the active page or VFX look. What it does NOT do: name played chords natively; Push needs a third-party Max for Live device for that, which is the closest prior art to our chordview. Its lights follow Live's clock, not arbitrary system audio. I found no equivalent published spec for Push 3 in this pass.

items.point: Novation Launchpad, Launchkey MK4, Components and Apollo Studio. Steal: device-side, clock-synced flash and pulse; a web app that talks to hardware over Web MIDI; a virtual on-screen twin for authoring light shows without the hardware.
items.detail: Launchpad X: channel 1 is a static colour, channel 2 flashes and channel 3 pulses, synced to MIDI beat clock (falling back to 120 bpm or the last clock). That makes beat lights cost almost no packets. Novation Components runs in Chrome or Edge through Web MIDI, which is direct precedent for 'a web page drives the keyboard'. The Launchkey MK4 OLED separates stationary displays from event-triggered temporary ones, and also takes custom bitmaps. Its Chord Map puts 8 chords of the chosen scale on the pads. Apollo Studio (open source) gives full-RGB light shows and a virtual Launchpad to work on away from the device; our keylab88mk3.js twin is the same idea. What they do NOT do: the Launchkey screen names chords from its own modes, and the SOS review mentions no recognition of free playing. Lights follow the DAW or clock, never system audio.

items.point: Scaler 3 and Captain Chords. Steal: chord candidates ranked with reasons (Scaler Detector), and one shared progression feeding every generator, played one key per chord with MIDI out (Captain Play). For the pads, that means a Chord-Map-style palette of the detected key's chords.
items.detail: What they do NOT do: drive controller hardware. Per users on Scaler's forum, Scaler 3 cannot show its chord or scale on NI's Light Guide or screen because it is not NKS-compliant, and the earlier house review notes 'no hardware MIDI out'. Captain Play outputs MIDI but lights nothing. Neither reads system audio for lights.

items.point: Hooktheory and Chordify. Steal: colour equals harmonic function in the key, so pads re-colour meaningfully when the key changes. Chordify's beat-synced bar grid with a moving cursor is the model for the chord timeline.
items.detail: Hookpad colours I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi and vii° red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple and pink, with a 'diatonic centric' and a 'major centric' mode. Our chordview colours by chord quality and interval role instead (chordview.py ROLE_COLORS and QUALITY_COLORS). Function colour would be a third scheme and the most adaptive one. Constraint: the KeyLab LCD only takes widget templates (lines, lists, popups), so a Chordify-style grid has to be text there (for example '| Cmaj7 | Am9 | Dm7 G13 |'), and the full timeline belongs on the web page. What they do NOT do: light hardware or follow a live keyboard performance.

items.point: Synthesia. Steal: separate the meaning of a light from the device that shows it. Synthesia sends a device-neutral 'key lights' MIDI stream (for example 'Finger-based channel', where the MIDI channel encodes the hand), and SynthesiaKontrol translates that stream to NI's Light Guide over USB.
items.detail: SynthesiaKontrol is MIT-licensed and active (pushed 2026-10-05). For us: the house emits one light-intent stream (pitch class, role, colour token, hold time), and adapters render it on the KeyLab pads, a future WLED strip, Hue, or the web twin. That stream would be the contract between the web pages and the keyboard. What Synthesia does NOT do: chords, audio-driven lights, or hosting.

items.point: LedFx, WLED Sound Reactive and Hue. Steal: one analysis broadcast to many renderers; virtual surfaces that span devices; named transitions between looks; lookahead light scripts when the track is known in advance.
items.detail: LedFx: a 'virtual' spreads one effect across segments of several devices or copies it onto each, with a per-virtual frequency range, transitions (Add, Dissolve, Push, Slide, Iris, Through White and others), gradient colour sources and scenes. Our pads, LCD accent, piano page and VFX bench could each be a virtual. WLED Sound Reactive multicasts audio features over UDP (239.0.0.1:11988) so many nodes share one analysis: broadcast the features, not pixels. Hue with Spotify builds a light script from track metadata and 'knows the song before you hear it'. For local files or FL renders, an offline beat and section pass gives the same lookahead, so lights can anticipate a drop. Hue Entertainment streams over DTLS-PSK UDP, up to 10 lights per packet at up to 25 Hz. What they do NOT do: drive controller pads or screens, or colour by harmony; they react to energy and bands (Hue also to mood and genre metadata), never to the chord being played.

items.point: Carla, Pedalboard and DawDreamer (hosting). Steal: Carla's OSC remote control and out-of-process plugin bridges (a crashing VST cannot kill the host), and Pedalboard and DawDreamer's state-as-bytes round trip.
items.detail: Carla hosts LADSPA, DSSI, LV2, VST2, VST3, AU, SF2/3 and SFZ, with rack and patchbay modes, OSC remote control, MIDI-CC automation and experimental bridges. Pedalboard handles VST3 on Windows (and AU on Mac, no VST2). It exposes raw_state and preset_data (.vstpreset bytes); show_editor must run on the main thread and blocks. AudioStream applies effects to live audio, but instruments render from a list of MIDI messages, and I found no documented path for live MIDI into an instrument. DawDreamer has load_preset(.fxp), load_vst3_preset and save_state/load_state. Licences: Pedalboard and PyFLP are GPL-3.0; Carla is GPL (GitHub shows no licence field). The repo is Apache-2.0, so run these as separate processes or reimplement the ideas. What they do NOT do: import FL presets, use a controller screen, or know about chords.

items.point: FL Studio preset round-trip. Steal: FL's own interchange paths. For VST2 that is .fxp/.fxb export from the plugin wrapper; .fst is FL's chunked state file that wraps the plugin's state blob; PyFLP reads .fst.
items.detail: Per a forum thread, FL cannot save .fxp for VST3 plugins, so VST3 has to go through .vstpreset or the raw chunk. The claim that .fst uses FLhd/FLdt chunks with an embedded VST blob comes from a secondary converter site (medium confidence). PyFLP is GPL-3.0, last pushed 2026-02-16. FL's Python MIDI scripting API (device_*.py files) is where Arturia's own KeyLab script lives and where our protocol was read from (arsenal/keylab/README.md, 'Why / provenance'). This pass found no tool that moves .fst presets into a standalone host and back, so the round-trip is a genuine gap.

items.point: Bitwig controller API and its open KeyLab mk3 extension. Steal: lights as functions of state, flushed only on change, with modes as layers. Also: Bitwig's MIT-licensed KeyLab mk3 source is a second protocol reference our code has never used.
items.detail: The Bitwig source agrees with ours on the header F0 00 20 6B 7F 42, DAW connect '00 02 05 01', screen '00 02 04 <target>' and pad bank '00 02 06 01'. Its screen targets include 0x0A (one line), 0x0C (two lines), 0x17-0x19 (popups of one to three lines), 0x1C (knob popup) and 0x1E (fader popup). Its RGB LED command is 'F0 00 20 6B 7F 42 04 02 03 <id> R G B 00 F7'. That first byte is 0x04; ours is 0x02, taken from FL, and the README's open question only weighed 0x00 against 0x02. Bitwig also defines BlinkState {BLINK1=0, BLINK2=1, BLINK3=2, PULSING=3, NONE=0x20}, yet its apply() writes 0. Whether device-side pulse works is therefore unbenched; if it does, beat lights could run on the device the way Launchpad and Push pulse. A grep of arsenal/keylab finds no reference to Bitwig or saxofonbrian. What Bitwig does NOT do: chord recognition, audio-driven lights, or web pages.

items.point: Arturia MIDI Control Center and Analog Lab. Steal: two protocol families that ignore each other, Arturia mode (00 01 04, used by Analog Lab) and DAW mode (00 02 04), so our DAW-family software can coexist with Analog Lab. Also the touch-to-reveal popups and the 8 contextual buttons under the screen.
items.detail: Arturia's overview lists a 3.5-inch 480x320 colour screen, 12 RGB pads with velocity and pressure, 9 touch-sensitive encoders and faders that show their value on touch, Chord/Scale/Arp modes, 6 user programs, MCU/HUI, and DAW scripts for FL, Live, Logic, Cubase, Bitwig and MainStage. What it does NOT do: name what you play (Chord mode generates chords, it does not recognise them), sync lights to audio, draw arbitrary graphics, or take content from a web page.

items.point: saxofonbrian/keylab-mk3-sysex: our closest twin and a free cross-check. It is a reverse-engineered map of KeyLab 61/88 mk3 screen SysEx, CC maps and LED IDs, with an Ableton plus Max for Live proof of concept.
items.detail: It covers list widgets (title 0x28, items 0x15, cursor), a fader readout (0x1D) and a button packet with RGB and a label. Text is plain ASCII 32-126. Its rate rule: two back-to-back 00 02 04 packets race and one is dropped, so queue them 60 ms apart; large SysEx bursts freeze the keyboard until a power cycle. That matches our own 12-packet ceiling in ledframe.py. Its proof of concept is DAW navigation (arm buttons, a locator list, the jog wheel), not chords or light.

items.point: Architecture constraint: web pages must not write to the keyboard directly. One local agent should own the KeyLab (NI's pattern) and pages send it intents.

items.detail: Since Chrome 124, every Web MIDI request shows a permission prompt, with SysEx bundled in. The house pages request sysex:false. Windows MIDI Services makes every port multi-client, and it is running here. So the page, FL and a Python daemon could all write to the DAW port at once, and screen packets would be dropped silently (the 60 ms race) rather than refused with 'port busy'. NI solves this with NIHostIntegrationAgent as the single owner of screens and lights. The same shape here: the keylab agent owns the port, paces packets and arbitrates who holds the screen, and the piano and VFX pages send light-intent and screen-intent messages over the local server.

items.point: Already done well elsewhere (adopt, do not reinvent)
items.detail: (1) Scale and chord-mode pad and key lighting: NI, Push, Maschine, Launchkey Chord Map, the KeyLab's own modes. (2) Named parameter pages from plugin metadata: NKS. (3) VST2/VST3 hosting and state as bytes: Carla, Pedalboard, DawDreamer, Komplete Kontrol. (4) Audio-reactive LEDs with bands, gradients, transitions and multi-device spans: LedFx, WLED SR, Hue Sync. (5) Beat-synced chord timelines and function colours: Chordify, Hookpad. (6) Clock-synced device-side pad animation and authored light shows: Launchpad, Push, Apollo Studio. (7) Configuring hardware from a web page: Novation Components. (8) The KeyLab mk3 screen and LED protocol itself: FL's script, Bitwig's MIT source, saxofonbrian's MIT map.

items.point: Genuinely novel (nothing found in this pass)
items.detail: (1) Recognising freely played, pedal-aware chords and showing the name on a controller's own screen with harmonic colours on its pads. Native nowhere; the only prior art is a third-party Max for Live device on Push. (2) Controller pads that follow the beat of any system audio (Spotify, YouTube, FL) through loopback. LedFx does this for LED strips, and controllers only follow DAW clock. (3) Visual web apps (piano visualizer, VFX bench) writing live content to a hardware screen and lights, with colour flowing both ways between page theme and pads. Web tools today only configure hardware. (4) Round-tripping FL .fst presets through a standalone host: no tool found. (5) One harmonic colour language shared by keyboard, pads, LCD, web pages and room lights. Each surface exists alone today, but nothing ties them to the chord being played. The novelty is in the integration, not in any single primitive.
